name: Shadow AI in Legal Teams
title: Shadow AI in Legal Teams
answer: Shadow AI in legal teams covers any use of artificial intelligence tools by lawyers, paralegals, legal operations staff, or outside counsel without review or approval from the firm's or department's security, privacy, and legal operations functions. It includes general purpose chatbots, drafting assistants, summarization tools, contract review add ons, transcription services, and AI features embedded in software that is already approved for other purposes. The category also reaches personal accounts, free tiers, browser extensions, and mobile apps that touch client confidences, matter files, or privileged communications. Because the site tracks 732 AI tools, the surface area is broad and changes quickly. The scope is not the technology alone, it is the gap between what staff actually use and what the organization has assessed.

sections.body: Shadow AI in legal teams covers any use of artificial intelligence tools by lawyers, paralegals, legal operations staff, or outside counsel without review or approval from the firm's or department's security, privacy, and legal operations functions. It includes general purpose chatbots, drafting assistants, summarization tools, contract review add ons, transcription services, and AI features embedded in software that is already approved for other purposes. The category also reaches personal accounts, free tiers, browser extensions, and mobile apps that touch client confidences, matter files, or privileged communications. Because the site tracks 732 AI tools, the surface area is broad and changes quickly. The scope is not the technology alone, it is the gap between what staff actually use and what the organization has assessed.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Shadow AI usually runs on cloud services, vendor APIs, browser extensions, desktop and mobile apps, and embedded features inside document management, email, practice management, and e-discovery platforms. Access often begins with a personal account, a free trial, or a plug in that a user installs without a procurement review. Data may leave the firm through prompts, uploaded files, meeting recordings, or connected drives, and it may be stored or used for model training under consumer terms. Some tools run locally on a laptop, which can still create risk if the device is unmanaged or the output is pasted into client work. The infrastructure is therefore a mix of sanctioned enterprise systems and unsanctioned endpoints, accounts, and integrations.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Security and legal operations teams discover shadow AI through single sign on logs, cloud access security brokers, endpoint agents, network traffic analysis, expense reports, and surveys or interviews with practice groups. They then triage each finding by data sensitivity, user role, client matter, and vendor terms, and they separate low risk experimentation from use that touches privileged or regulated data. Audits often combine technical evidence with policy review, training records, and checks against outside counsel guidelines. The work is iterative because new tools appear and existing tools add AI features without a new purchase. A common output is a register of observed tools, owners, data flows, and open questions for security, privacy, and the general counsel's office.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The core governance questions are whether client data was transmitted, whether privilege was preserved, whether the vendor's terms permit confidentiality and deletion, and whether the output can be traced to a source. Legal teams also face professional responsibility rules on competence, confidentiality, supervision, and communication, plus contractual duties in engagement letters and outside counsel guidelines. Provenance matters because AI generated text, citations, and images may be inaccurate or may incorporate third party material, and the site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, along with 29 AI case law precedents. The site also tracks 219 compliance and regulation pages, which show how quickly duties are shifting across jurisdictions and sectors. The practical record keeping includes prompts, outputs, model versions, retention periods, and the basis for any client consent.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Shadow AI in legal teams is likely to become less about obvious chatbots and more about invisible features inside approved platforms, so discovery will depend on vendor transparency and contract terms. Expect more client audits, outside counsel guidelines that ask about AI use, and insurance questions about data handling and model provenance. The site's tracking of 6979 state AI bills suggests a widening compliance map, even if many bills never become law. Firms and legal departments will keep separating approved tools from unsanctioned use, and the boundary will move as vendors add AI to existing products. The open question is whether governance can keep pace with adoption without blocking useful work.
